topicName: Join Strategies (Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding PostgreSQL Join Strategies: Nested Loop, Hash Join, and Merge Join"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you execute a SQL query involving joins, the PostgreSQL query planner evaluates multiple algorithms to determine the most efficient way to combine rows from two or more relations. Understanding these join strategies is crucial for query optimization and database tuning."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"1. Nested Loop Join"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Nested Loop join is the simplest join strategy. For every row in the outer table, PostgreSQL scans the inner table to find matching rows. While this can be slow for large unindexed tables, it becomes extremely efficient when the inner table is indexed on the join column."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"How Nested Loop Works"},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Iterates through the driving (outer) relation row by row."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"For each outer row, it searches the inner relation for matching records."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Frequently utilizes an index scan on the inner table to avoid sequential scans."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"-- Example query that often triggers a Nested Loop Join
SELECT * FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.id = 42;"},{"order":10,"type":"heading","text":"2. Hash Join"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Hash Join is typically used for large, unsorted datasets. PostgreSQL reads the smaller relation (the build input) and builds an in-memory hash table using the join key. It then scans the larger relation (the probe input), hashes the join key of each row, and probes the hash table to find matches."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Characteristics of Hash Joins"},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Requires an equality condition (=) in the join predicate."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Performance depends heavily on work_mem; if the hash table exceeds work_mem, PostgreSQL writes data to disk (batches and batches spilling)."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"-- Example query ideal for Hash Join
SELECT * FROM large_sales s
JOIN large_products p ON s.product_id = p.product_id;"},{"order":16,"type":"heading","text":"3. Merge Join"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Merge Join requires both input relations to be sorted on the join key. PostgreSQL reads through both sorted streams simultaneously, matching rows as it goes. If the data is not already sorted via an index, PostgreSQL may add an explicit Sort node to the execution plan."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Characteristics of Merge Joins"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Highly efficient for very large datasets when data is already sorted (e.g., via B-Tree indexes)."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Supports inequality operators like <, <=, >, >= in addition to equality."},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"-- Example query that may use Merge Join
SELECT * FROM employees e
JOIN salaries s ON e.emp_id = s.emp_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id;"},{"order":22,"type":"heading","text":"Analyzing Joins with EXPLAIN"},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"Always use the EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE command to inspect which join strategy the PostgreSQL query planner has chosen for your query."},{"order":24,"type":"code","text":"EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;"}]
